reason: Literally means "children's garden." Coined by educator Friedrich Fröbel in the 1840s to describe his new approach to early childhood education.
Borrowed from French "ballet," itself from Italian "balletto," a diminutive of "ballo" meaning "dance." Ballet as an art form developed in the Italian and French royal courts.
A direct borrowing of the Japanese word for the dish, which traditionally refers to vinegared rice rather than the raw fish itself.
Short for "pianoforte," Italian for "soft-loud," describing the instrument's ability to play both quiet and loud notes, unlike the harpsichord.
Coined by Czech writer Karel Čapek in his 1920 play R.U.R., from the Czech word "robota" meaning forced labor or drudgery.
Literally "harbor wave," combining "tsu" (harbor) and "nami" (wave), describing how the waves become dangerous specifically near the coast.
From Sanskrit "yoga," meaning union or discipline, related to the practice of joining body and mind in ancient Indian philosophy.
A blend of Japanese "kara" (empty) and "okesutora" (orchestra), literally meaning "empty orchestra" — music without the original vocals.
From Arabic "al-kuhl," originally referring to a fine powder used as eye makeup, later applied to distilled substances by European alchemists.
Believed to come from Hokkien Chinese "kê-tsiap," a fermented fish sauce, which spread through Southeast Asia before European traders adapted it into the tomato-based sauce known today.
From Dutch "koekje," meaning "little cake," brought to America by Dutch settlers in New York.
From Dutch "baas," meaning master or foreman, adopted into American English partly because "master" carried unwanted associations with slavery.
From Sanskrit "avatara," meaning "descent," originally referring to the earthly incarnation of a Hindu deity, later adapted to mean a digital representation of a person.
From Japanese "taikun," meaning "great lord," a title used for the shogun. It entered English through American diplomats in the 1850s and 60s.
From the Hungarian town of Kocs, famous for building horse-drawn carriages in the 15th century. The meaning later extended to "someone who guides you," giving us the modern sense of a sports coach.
Literally "little fly" in Spanish, a diminutive of "mosca" (fly).
From Nahuatl "xocolatl," a bitter drink made from cacao beans consumed by the Aztecs long before sugar was added by Europeans.
From Nahuatl "tomatl," the Aztec word for the fruit, which spread to Europe after Spanish colonization of the Americas.
From Sanskrit "guru," meaning teacher or spiritual guide, literally translating to something close to "weighty" or "venerable."
From Hindi "champo," meaning "to massage," introduced to English speakers in colonial India before becoming associated specifically with hair washing.
From "bangla," meaning "of Bengal," describing a style of low, single-story house common in that region of India.
From "pajama," a loose-fitting leg garment tied at the waist, adopted by British colonists in India before becoming standard English sleepwear.
Literally "empty hand," reflecting that the martial art is practiced without weapons.
From Inuktitut "iglu," which actually just means "house" in general, not specifically a snow dwelling.
From Swahili "safari," meaning journey, which itself comes from the Arabic word "safar" for travel.
German for "fear" or "anxiety," adopted into English largely through 20th-century psychology and philosophy to describe a deep, often existential dread.
From the Inuit word for a small, covered boat originally made from animal skins stretched over a wooden frame, used for hunting on Arctic waters.
From "serge de Nîmes," a sturdy fabric originally made in the French city of Nîmes.
From "Gênes," the French name for the Italian city of Genoa, where a similar cotton fabric was originally produced.
Literally "bread and butter table," describing the traditional Swedish buffet of many small dishes served together.
Originally a printing term for a pre-cast metal plate used to repeatedly print the same image, extended to mean an overused expression.
French for "coffee," which itself traces back further to Arabic "qahwa" — the word for the drink became the name for the place that served it.
From French "entreprendre," meaning "to undertake," describing someone who organizes and takes on the risk of a business venture.
Literally "present yourselves," from the French command form, describing an agreed meeting time and place.
Named after Étienne de Silhouette, an 18th-century French finance minister known for cheap, quickly-made portrait outlines during his brief and unpopular time in office.
From Italian for "pressed out," describing how the coffee is forced through finely-ground beans under pressure.
A direct borrowing from Italian, referring to the flatbread dish that originated in Naples.
From "Vulcano," an Italian island named after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire, believed by ancient peoples to be his forge.
From Italian "ombrella," a diminutive of "ombra" meaning shade, since umbrellas were first used to block the sun rather than rain.
From Italian "balcone," describing a platform projecting from a building's upper floor.
A diminutive of Italian "casa" (house), originally meaning a small country house or social club before taking on its gambling association.
Originally referred to the sugared almonds thrown during Italian carnival celebrations, later replaced by paper but keeping the name.
Literally "bottle" in Italian; the connection to failure comes from an old theatrical phrase for a performance that flopped, though the exact origin story is debated.
From Italian "graffiare," meaning "to scratch," originally describing markings scratched into ancient walls before referring to modern spray paint art.
Named after Paparazzo, an aggressive photographer character in Federico Fellini's 1960 film La Dolce Vita.
From Italian "studio," meaning a room for study, which came to describe artists' and later film and recording workspaces.
From Arabic "sifr" (meaning "empty"), which passed into Italian as "zefiro" and then into English, tracking the number's spread from Indian and Arabic mathematics into Europe.
From "al-jabr," part of the title of a 9th-century mathematical text by Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi, meaning "the reunion of broken parts."
From Arabic "sukkar," which itself traces back to Sanskrit "sharkara," following the sugar trade from India through the Arab world to Europe.
From Arabic "qahwa," via Turkish "kahve," describing the drink first cultivated in the Arabian Peninsula and Ethiopia.
From Arabic "makhazin," meaning storehouses; the word originally referred to a place for storing goods before coming to mean a periodical "storehouse" of articles.
From Arabic "suffah," describing a raised platform or bench covered with cushions.
From Arabic "zarafa," the origin of which is uncertain but which passed into English through Italian and French.
From Arabic "qutn," reflecting how the cotton trade and the plant itself reached Europe through Arabic-speaking traders.
From Arabic "amir al-" (commander of), a title picked up during the Crusades and later applied specifically to naval commanders.
Likely influenced by both Chinese "tai fung" (great wind) and Greek "typhon" (a mythological storm giant), blending together as the word entered English.
From Cantonese "gong fu," originally referring to skill or achievement gained through hard work and time, not martial arts specifically.
From the Min Nan Chinese word "te," spread to Europe by Dutch traders — while Mandarin-influenced trade routes gave other languages words closer to "cha."
Adapted from Chinese "lamian" (pulled noodles), the dish and its name were popularized in Japan before spreading worldwide as "ramen."
From Japanese "e" (picture) and "moji" (character); the resemblance to the English word "emotion" is a coincidence.
From "ori" (fold) and "kami" (paper), describing the traditional art of paper folding.
Short for "suji wa dokushin ni kagiru," meaning "the numbers must remain single," though the puzzle format itself was actually invented in the United States.
From Japanese "futon," describing a traditional padded mattress that could be rolled up and stored during the day.
From "hancho," meaning "squad leader," picked up by American soldiers stationed in Japan after World War II.
From Cantonese "wok," the name for the round-bottomed pan used throughout Chinese cooking.
From "nin" (to endure or sneak) and "ja" (person), describing the covert agents and mercenaries of feudal Japan.
From a verb meaning "to serve," describing the hereditary warrior class who served Japan's feudal lords.
The Japanese pronunciation of Chinese "Chan," which itself derives from Sanskrit "dhyana," meaning meditation — tracing a path from India through China to Japan.
From "bon" (tray) and "sai" (planting), describing the art of growing miniature trees in shallow containers.
From "man" (mind) and "tra" (instrument), describing a sacred sound or phrase repeated in meditation.
From Sanskrit "karman," meaning "action" or "deed," central to the idea that actions have consequences across lifetimes in Hindu and Buddhist thought.
Literally "blown out" or "extinguished," describing the Buddhist state of liberation from suffering and desire.
From Hindi "lut," meaning goods seized by force, adopted by British soldiers and officials during colonial rule in India.
From Hindi "jangal," originally meaning wasteland or forest, later narrowed in English to specifically mean dense tropical forest.
From Hindi "thag," originally referring to a member of a historical band of professional robbers and stranglers in India.
Possibly from Hindi "varanda," itself likely borrowed from Portuguese, describing a covered porch attached to a house.
Believed to come from Hindi "panch," meaning "five," referring to the traditional five ingredients (spirit, water, lemon, sugar, and spice) used in the drink.
From Hindi "pandit," meaning a learned scholar or teacher, especially one versed in Sanskrit and Hindu law.
From Hindi "chita," ultimately from Sanskrit, meaning "speckled" or "variegated," describing the animal's spotted coat.
Traces back through Arabic and Persian to Sanskrit "khanda," meaning a piece of sugar, following the spread of sugar refining from India.
From Old Persian "pairidaeza," meaning "walled garden," originally describing the lush enclosed parks of Persian royalty.
From Persian "bazar," meaning marketplace, describing the traditional covered markets found across the Middle East and South Asia.
From Persian "karwan," describing a group of travelers, often traders, journeying together for safety across long distances.
From Persian "shah," meaning "king," the central piece of the game, which reached Europe through Arabic and Old French.
From Persian "shah mat," meaning "the king is helpless" or "the king is dead," marking the end of a chess game.
Traces back through Persian and Arabic to Sanskrit "naranga," the name for the fruit, following its spread westward along trade routes.
From Urdu and Persian "khak," meaning "dust" or "earth," describing the dust-colored fabric first used by British colonial troops in India.
A diminutive of Russian "voda," meaning "water," literally translating to something like "little water."
Borrowed by Russian from a Sami or Finnish word for a treeless, frozen plain, describing the Arctic landscape.
From Russian "mamont," possibly derived from a Siberian indigenous word, describing the massive extinct elephant relative found preserved in the region's ice.
From Russian "troe," meaning "three," originally describing a traditional carriage pulled by three horses side by side.
The lively dance likely takes its name from the Czech word "pulka," meaning "half-step," describing its characteristic quick footwork.
From German "Brezel," ultimately from Latin "brachiatus" (having branches or arms), describing the twisted, arm-like shape of the bread.
Named after Hamburg, Germany, where a style of minced beef patty was associated with the city before German immigrants popularized it in the United States.
A direct compound of German "wandern" (to hike or wander) and "Lust" (desire), describing a strong urge to travel.
From German "Doppel" (double) and "Gänger" (goer), literally meaning "double-walker," describing a look-alike or ghostly double of a living person.
From German "poltern" (to make noise or rumble) and "Geist" (ghost or spirit), describing a noisy, mischievous ghost.
From German "walzen," meaning "to turn" or "to roll," describing the dance's characteristic turning steps.
From German "Delikatessen," meaning delicacies or fine foods, itself borrowed from French "délicatesse."
From German "kaputt," meaning broken or ruined, popularized in English partly through soldiers returning from World War I and II.
Borrowed from an Aboriginal language of the Sydney region, referring to the curved throwing stick used for hunting.
From the Guugu Yimithirr language of northern Australia, referring specifically to a type of dark-colored kangaroo — the popular myth that it originally meant "I don't understand" is false.
From Tongan "tabu," meaning forbidden or sacred, introduced to English by explorer James Cook after his voyages in the Pacific.
From Polynesian "tatau," describing the traditional practice of marking the skin, also introduced to English through James Cook's Pacific voyages.
From an Algonquian language of eastern North America, meaning "twig eater," describing the animal's browsing habits.
From Taino "hurakan," the name of a storm god, adopted by Spanish colonizers in the Caribbean before entering English.
From Taino "barbacoa," describing a wooden framework used for cooking or sleeping, adapted by Spanish colonizers to describe outdoor cooking over an open fire.
A compound of German "Schaden" (harm) and "Freude" (joy), describing the pleasure someone feels at another person's misfortune.
From German "Zeit" (time) and "Geist" (spirit), meaning the defining mood or spirit of a particular era.
Short for "Blitzkrieg" (lightning war), a German military term that entered English during World War II and later broadened to mean any sudden, intense effort.
Literally "health" in German, said after someone sneezes as a wish for their wellbeing, much like "bless you."
From German "Rücken" (back) and "Sack" (bag), describing a bag carried on the back.
A diminutive of Swiss German "Mues" (puree or mush), describing the breakfast dish created by a Swiss physician in the early 1900s.
Named after Rudolf Diesel, the German engineer who invented the diesel engine in the 1890s.
Named after Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, the German physicist who proposed the temperature scale in 1724.
Named after the German city of Köln (Cologne), where the fragrance known as "eau de Cologne" was first produced in the 18th century.
French for "crescent," describing the pastry's curved shape.
From French "restaurer" (to restore), since early establishments were known for serving restorative broths and soups.
From French "bouquet," originally meaning a small wood or grove, later coming to describe a bunch of flowers.
Originally referred to the coarse woolen cloth ("bure") used to cover writing desks, before the word came to mean the desk itself and later an office.
French for "stylish" or "elegant," borrowed into English largely unchanged in both spelling and meaning.
From French "étiquette," originally meaning a small ticket or label, which came to refer to the rules of proper court behavior posted for guests to follow.
From French "face," describing the front of a building, later extended to mean a deceptive outward appearance.
From French "fiancer," meaning "to promise," describing someone promised in marriage.
From French "naïf," ultimately from Latin "nativus" (natural or native), describing an innocent, unworldly quality.
From French "souvenir," meaning "to remember," describing an object kept as a memory of a place or event.
Literally "one who heats," originally referring to the person who stoked the boiler of early steam-powered cars.
French for "kitchen" or "cooking style," borrowed to describe a particular tradition of food and cooking.
From French "garer," meaning "to shelter" or "to dock," originally used for sheltering boats before referring to storing cars.
From French "béret," ultimately from a word for a type of woolen cap traditionally worn in the Basque and Béarn regions.
Named after the Champagne region of France, the only place sparkling wine can legally be called by this name.
From French "hôpital ambulant" (walking hospital), describing mobile field hospitals that followed armies before the word narrowed to mean the vehicle itself.
French for "blow" or "strike," used in English mainly in "coup d'état," literally "a strike against the state."
From French "dépôt," meaning a place where things are deposited or stored, later applied to train and bus stations.
Popularized by French, though it likely traces back further to Arabic "mass," meaning "to touch" or "to feel."
From French "salon," meaning a large reception room, originally referring to fashionable social gatherings before narrowing to mean a beauty business.
The feminine form of Italian "ballerino" (dancer), from "ballare," to dance.
Italian for "fresh," describing the technique of painting on wet, or "fresh," plaster.
From Venetian Italian, describing the narrow, flat-bottomed boats used to navigate the canals of Venice.
Italian for "work," specifically referring to a dramatic work set to music.
Italian for a public square or open space in a city, often surrounded by buildings.
From Venetian Italian, originally describing a gondola race on the city's canals before broadening to mean any boat race.
From Italian "sopra" (above), describing the highest singing voice range.
Italian for "room" or "stopping place," describing a grouped section of lines in a poem.
Italian for "time," describing the speed at which a piece of music is played.
From Latin "villa," a country house or estate, passed into English through Italian usage.
The plural of Italian "broccolo," meaning "the flowering top of a cabbage."
The plural of Italian "spaghetto," a diminutive of "spago" (string or twine), describing the pasta's thin shape.
The plural of Italian "zucchino," a diminutive of "zucca" (squash or gourd).
From Sicilian Italian, originally describing boldness or bravado before becoming associated specifically with organized crime networks.
Named for its color resembling the brown hooded robes worn by Capuchin friars.
Italian for "frozen," describing the dense, slow-churned style of Italian ice cream.
From Hindi "bandhnu," describing a method of tie-dying cloth that produces a distinctive spotted pattern.
From Hindi "bangri," describing a rigid bracelet, often glass or metal, worn around the wrist.
From Hindi "chatni," describing a spiced condiment made from fruits, vegetables, or herbs.
From Hindi and Persian "kamarband," meaning "waistband," adopted by British colonial officers as formal dress.
From "Mughal," referring to the Muslim dynasty that ruled much of India, later extended in English to mean any powerful, influential figure.
From Persian "shal," describing a piece of fabric worn over the shoulders, originally associated with the Kashmir region.
Traces through Greek "tigris" back to a Persian or Iranian source, believed to be related to a word meaning "arrow," describing the animal's swift movement.
From Persian "nilak" (bluish), passed through Arabic and French before arriving in English as the name of both the flower and its pale purple color.
From Persian "nan," simply meaning "bread," describing the soft, leavened flatbread now associated with South Asian cuisine.
From Persian "kabab," describing grilled or roasted meat, a word shared and adapted widely across the Middle East, Turkey, and South Asia.
From Arabic "falafil," describing the deep-fried patties made from ground chickpeas or fava beans.
Arabic for "chickpeas," the main ingredient in the popular chickpea and tahini dip.
From Arabic "shaykh," originally meaning "elder" or "old man," used as a title of respect for a leader or tribal chief.
From Arabic "haram," meaning "forbidden" or "sacred," describing a private, protected part of a household.
From Arabic "jinni," describing a supernatural spirit in Islamic mythology, later popularized in English through translations of the One Thousand and One Nights.
From Arabic "al-iksir," describing a substance alchemists believed could turn base metals into gold or grant eternal life.
From Arabic "sharab," meaning "a drink," related to the same root that gave English the word "sherbet."
From Arabic "matrah," meaning "the place where something is thrown down," describing a place to lie down and sleep.
From Arabic "mawsim," meaning "season," describing the seasonal winds and rains of South and Southeast Asia.
From Arabic "ta'rif," meaning "notification" or "a making known," describing a published list of prices or duties.
From Arabic "al-qubba" (the vault or dome), passed through Spanish "alcoba" to describe a recessed section of a room.
From Arabic "al-'ud," literally "the wood," describing the stringed instrument that spread into Europe through Islamic Spain.
From Persian "sharbat," a cooling drink, itself related to the Arabic root for "to drink" that also gave English "syrup" and "coffee."
Named after a crude horn-like musical instrument invented by comedian Bob Burns, whose shape resembled the World War II anti-tank weapon.
From an Algonquian language of eastern North America, describing the animal known for its strong-smelling spray.
From an Algonquian word roughly meaning "one who scratches with the hands," describing the animal's dexterous front paws.
From an Ojibwe word describing the small striped squirrel, possibly related to the sound of its chattering call.
From an Arawakan language of the Caribbean, describing a narrow boat propelled by paddles, first encountered by Spanish explorers.
Derived from "Caniba," a name Spanish explorers used for the Carib people, based on reports (of disputed accuracy) that they ate human flesh.
From Taino "batata," originally referring to the sweet potato, later applied more broadly after Spanish colonization.
A direct borrowing from Finnish, describing the traditional steam bathhouse central to Finnish culture for centuries.
From Old Norse "hreindyri," combining a word for the animal with "dyr" (deer), reflecting Scandinavian familiarity with the species.
From Swedish "ombud" (representative) and "man," describing an official appointed to investigate complaints against institutions.
From Norwegian dialect words meaning "sloping track," describing the skiing technique of weaving between markers.
From Old Norse "fjörðr," describing the long, narrow, steep-sided inlets carved by glaciers along the Norwegian coast.
Named after Geysir, a specific hot spring in Iceland whose name comes from an Old Norse verb meaning "to gush."
From Chinese "gonghe," part of the name of Chinese industrial cooperatives, adopted by U.S. Marines in the 1940s to mean "work together" and later "overly enthusiastic."
Literally "wind" and "water," describing the traditional Chinese practice of arranging spaces in harmony with natural energy flow.
From Chinese "doufu," meaning "bean curd," the food and its name spread first to Japan and then worldwide.
From Cantonese "wan tan," describing the small dumplings, often served in soup.
From Japanese "umai" (delicious) and "mi" (taste), describing the savory "fifth taste" identified by a Japanese chemist in 1908.
Japanese for "alcohol" broadly, though in English it specifically refers to the traditional fermented rice wine.
From Japanese "man" (whimsical) and "ga" (pictures), describing Japanese comics and graphic novels.
A shortened Japanese pronunciation of the English word "animation," now referring specifically to Japanese-produced animated works.
From "sen" (before) and "sei" (life/born), literally meaning "one born before," used as a respectful title for teachers and masters.
A modern English blend of "tofu" and "turkey," invented to describe a plant-based Thanksgiving alternative — included here as an example of how new loanword-influenced blends keep forming even today.
Named after Soviet foreign minister Vyacheslav Molotov; Finnish soldiers coined "Molotov cocktail" sarcastically during the 1939 Winter War.
Russian for "grandmother," which in English came to describe the type of headscarf traditionally worn by older Russian women.
From Hawaiian "wiki wiki," meaning "quick," chosen by the creator of the first wiki software because a shuttle bus with that name was fast.
Hawaiian for "jumping flea," possibly describing the quick finger movements used to play the small stringed instrument.
Hawaiian for a garland, traditionally made of flowers, leaves, or shells, given as a symbol of welcome or celebration.
A Hawaiian greeting meaning both "hello" and "goodbye," rooted in a deeper concept of love, peace, and compassion.
Hawaiian for the traditional dance form that uses movement and chant to tell stories.
Named after a Hawaiian dish of taro leaves, the word came to describe the entire traditional feast.
From Spanish "vainilla," a diminutive of "vaina" (pod or sheath), describing the plant's slender seed pod.
From Spanish "guitarra," which traces back through Arabic to the ancient Greek "kithara," an early stringed instrument.
From Spanish "rodear," meaning "to go around" or "to round up," describing the herding and competitive events of ranch life.
From Spanish "rancho," originally describing a small farm or group of farm laborers before broadening to mean any large cattle-raising property.
Spanish for an inner courtyard, borrowed directly to describe an outdoor paved area attached to a house.
Spanish for a public square, borrowed to describe an open urban gathering space.
Spanish for "party" or "celebration," often specifically referring to a festival tied to a religious holiday.
From Latin "sexta" (sixth hour), referring to the midday rest traditionally taken around noon in Spanish-speaking countries.
Spanish for "armed force," most famously associated with the Spanish Armada, the naval fleet sent against England in 1588.
From Spanish "cargar," meaning "to load," describing goods carried by a ship or vehicle.
From Spanish "embargar," meaning "to seize" or "to restrict," describing an official ban on trade with a country.
From Spanish "cigarro," possibly related to a Mayan word for smoking, reflecting the origins of tobacco use in the Americas.
From Spanish "cafetería," meaning "coffee shop," though the American self-serve dining concept it now describes developed separately.
From Spanish "el lagarto," meaning "the lizard," used by early Spanish explorers in the Americas to describe the large reptile.
Likely from Spanish "tronada" (thunderstorm), blended with "tornar" (to turn), describing the storm's violent rotation.
A diminutive of Spanish "guerra" (war), literally meaning "little war," describing small-scale, irregular combat tactics.
Spanish for "male," adopted into English to describe an exaggerated sense of masculine pride or toughness.
From Spanish "vigilante," meaning "watchman" or "vigilant," describing someone who takes law enforcement into their own hands.
From Spanish "adobar" (to plaster), itself from Arabic "al-tub" (the brick), describing sun-dried mud brick construction.
From Spanish "cañón," meaning "tube" or "pipe," describing the deep, narrow valleys carved by rivers.
Spanish for "friend," borrowed directly into casual English usage, especially in the American Southwest.
Spanish for "council" or "meeting," adopted into English specifically to describe a military group ruling a country after seizing power.
Spanish for "crazy" or "insane," borrowed largely unchanged into informal American English.
From an indigenous Araucanian language of Chile and Argentina, describing a blanket-like garment with a hole for the head, adopted into Spanish and then English.
From Spanish "mestengo" or "mesteño," meaning "wild" or "stray," describing the feral horses descended from Spanish stock in the Americas.
Spanish for "rough" or "rude," applied in the American West to describe an unbroken or wild horse.
From Nahuatl "cacahuatl," adapted by Spanish colonizers as "cacao," which later shifted in English to "cocoa."
From Nahuatl "ahuacatl," adapted by Spanish as "aguacate," and later reshaped in English into "avocado."
From Nahuatl "chilli," the name for the pepper, adopted largely unchanged as it spread through Spanish and into English.
From Nahuatl "coyotl," the name for the wild canine native to North America, adopted into Spanish and then English.
From Italian "violino," a diminutive of "viola," describing the smaller, higher-pitched instrument in the string family.
From Italian "tromba" (trumpet) with the augmentative suffix "-one," literally meaning "big trumpet."
From Italian "torso," originally describing a stalk or stump, later applied to ancient statues found without their limbs and head.
Italian for "goddess," originally used to describe celebrated female opera singers before broadening to describe any high-profile, demanding performer.
From French "motif," meaning "motive" or "theme," describing a recurring idea or pattern in art, music, or literature.
French for "kind" or "type," borrowed to describe categories of art, music, film, and literature.
A diminutive of French "brun" (brown), describing someone with brown hair.
From French "blond," describing fair or golden-colored hair; English retains the French feminine spelling "blonde" for women.
Literally "bottom of the bag" in French, describing a street closed at one end.
Literally "already seen" in French, describing the eerie feeling of having already experienced a current situation.
Believed to come from a Venetian word for a foundry district, since Venice's segregated Jewish quarter in the 1500s was located near an old iron foundry.
From Italian "motto," meaning "word" or "saying," describing a short phrase expressing a guiding principle.
From "ki" (to wear) and "mono" (thing), literally meaning "a thing to wear," describing the traditional Japanese garment.
From Portuguese "marmelada," a preserve originally made from quince ("marmelo"), later applied in English specifically to citrus preserves.
